title: Harbor and Uniform
premise: In 1898, in a colonial harbor town, Hazel Underhill—indentured since childhood to the Meridian Trading Company after their pearl-diver mother drowned—has learned that survival means being unremarkable. When an infant is abandoned at the company warehouse with a note ordering the face forgotten, Hazel recognizes the child as kin to the drowned divers whose deaths the company has been quietly erasing from its ledgers. As Hazel and a forged-papers clerk named Ivo trace the baby's parentage, they uncover a pattern of falsified death records covering a diving disaster the company caused. Racing against the sailing of the company ship carrying the true ledgers to be burned abroad, Hazel must smuggle testimony and documents into the hands of a visiting colonial magistrate before the morning tide—sacrificing their own invisibility, and nearly their freedom, to put the truth on the record.
about_author: Gideon Nystrom is a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing shipping ledgers in coastal repositories, where he first encountered the gaps left by victors' record-keeping. He writes historical fiction about the people history tried not to notice.

chapters.title: The Weight of Water
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. A day in the life of the Meridian warehouse: weighing pearl shell, dodging the overseer Brandt's attention, remembering a mother who taught her to hold her breath. Hazel explains her philosophy—history happens elsewhere, to people who matter. Emotional beat: the fragile comfort of deliberate invisibility, established so it can be broken.

chapters.title: Left at the Door
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. During a storm, a crying bundle appears on the warehouse step with a note: 'Forget the face.' Brandt orders it taken to the mission orphanage by morning. Hazel, holding the child, notices a diver's scarred amulet tucked in the blanket—one like her mother's. Emotional beat: the first crack in Hazel's practiced indifference; she hides the amulet instead of discarding it.

chapters.title: Ivo of the Second Drawer
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV introduces Ivo, a clerk who forges clean papers for the company and keeps a secret second drawer of his own history. Hazel asks him, casually, how one might find out who a child belongs to. Ivo warns her that questions are how indentured people disappear. Emotional beat: wary alliance; two people who survive by not asking, choosing to ask anyway.

chapters.title: What the Ledgers Don't Say
chapters.summary: Alternating Hazel and Ivo POV. Ivo discovers the diving-crew rolls for the wreck of the Cormorant list men as 'transferred' rather than drowned—and the transfer dates match the night the lighthouse was dark. The baby's amulet bears the mark of a diver listed as transferred. Emotional beat: dread hardening into purpose; the machinery of erasure becomes visible.

chapters.title: Brandt's Kindness
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Brandt unexpectedly promotes Hazel, offers better rations, and mentions the magistrate's ship arriving next week—the same ship that will carry sealed crates 'for disposal abroad.' His kindness feels like a leash. The baby, hidden with the cook Mrs. Ferro, grows stronger. Emotional beat: the seduction of comfort offered precisely when Hazel is most dangerous.

chapters.title: Mrs. Ferro's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Mrs. Ferro's POV. The cook reveals she has sheltered three such children over twenty years, each time told to forget a face, each time keeping instead a small token. She shows Hazel the tokens: a whole quiet archive of the erased. Emotional beat: revelation that Hazel was never alone in remembering—found family forms around shared refusal.

chapters.title: The Magistrate's Clerk
chapters.summary: Hazel and Ivo POV. They attempt to reach the visiting magistrate through his clerk, who listens politely and then reports them to Brandt—or so they believe. Ivo is detained for questioning about 'irregularities in the rolls.' Hazel realizes the clock is now measured in hours, not days. Emotional beat: betrayal and terror; the cost of visibility arrives early.

chapters.title: Everything That Floats
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. With Ivo imprisoned in the warehouse loft, Hazel plans the impossible: copy the true ledgers, free Ivo, and get everything aboard the magistrate's ship before the tide turns at dawn. Mrs. Ferro and the dockside divers—her mother's old community—offer boats, alibis, and muscle. Emotional beat: rising tension; invisibility inverted into a weapon, as no one ever thought to watch the invisible.

chapters.title: Before the Tide Turns
chapters.summary: Climax, Hazel's POV. Night raid: Hazel copies pages by lamplight while Brandt circles, frees Ivo through the loft hatch, and carries the testimony and the baby to the quay as the ship's bell rings. Confronted by Brandt at the gangplank, Hazel speaks the divers' names aloud—on the record, before witnesses—then steps aboard with the magistrate's clerk, revealed as an ally after all. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into testimony.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Resolution, Hazel's POV. Weeks later: the inquiry opens, the Cormorant's dead are restored to the rolls, and Brandt sails away under investigation. Hazel's indenture is voided; Mrs. Ferro keeps the kitchen, now openly raising the found children together. Hazel writes her mother's name into the public register herself. Emotional beat: grief honored, identity chosen—history happened here, to them, and now it belongs to them too.
